docs.title: Open STEM Hub
docs.text:
A curated, free-and-open collection of coding, electronics and robotics projects for ages 11–20+, built from parts you can actually buy.

Every resource here is free to access. Every project maps to components stocked by RS Components UK, The Pi Hut, Adafruit, Pimoroni or Kitronik. No paywalled courses, no "sign up to see the tutorial", no dead links (we check weekly — see link-check workflow).

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
New to this? Pick your entry point:

If you are… Go to A parent or teacher, unsure what to buy Buying guide (UK) Looking for projects by age Age bands & learning tracks Looking for projects by hardware you own Platforms Looking for projects by topic (robots, wearables, AI…) Themes Preparing for a competition Competitions Coming from LEGO MINDSTORMS or SPIKE ⚠️ Read this first Wanting to contribute CONTRIBUTING.md

No hardware yet and want to try anyway? Both Wokwi and Tinkercad Circuits simulate Arduino, Pi Pico and ESP32 in the browser for free. Half the projects here can be prototyped before you spend anything.

docs.title: Learning tracks
docs.text:
Three difficulty bands, each a sequence rather than a pile of links. Detail in docs/02-age-bands-and-tracks.md.

  • Foundation (≈11–13) — block coding, pre-made kits, crocodile clips. No soldering, no command line.
  • Intermediate (≈14–16) — MicroPython/CircuitPython, breadboards, first soldering, GitHub basics.
  • Advanced (≈17–20+) — Linux, C/C++, PCB design, ROS 2, on-device ML, version control as a habit.

Ages are a rough guide, not a gate. A motivated 12-year-old with support beats a disengaged 16-year-old every time.

docs.title: Claude Code Instructions for Open STEM Hub
docs.text: Welcome to the Open STEM Hub repository! This project curates free, accessible STEM projects (coding, electronics, robotics) for students.

docs.title: Workflows and Sub-Agents
docs.text:
We use specific, standardized workflows to maintain the quality and consistency of this repository. If you are asked to perform tasks related to curating, formatting, or validating resources, please read and strictly follow the corresponding "Sub-Agent" instruction files before proceeding:

  1. Resource Researcher
  2. Trigger: When asked to find, research, or discover new STEM projects.

  3. Instructions: Please read and follow .agents/skills/resource-researcher/SKILL.md

  4. Resource Formatter

  5. Trigger: When asked to format a resource link or text to be added to the repository.

  6. Instructions: Please read and follow .agents/skills/resource-formatter/SKILL.md

  7. Link Validator

  8. Trigger: When asked to verify, check, or validate a resource to see if it meets our accessibility standards.
  9. Instructions: Please read and follow .agents/skills/link-validator/SKILL.md

docs.title: General Project Constraints
docs.text:
• Free Access: Only accept resources that are completely free to access (no forced sign-ups or paywalls to read the core tutorial).
  • Target Audience: Ensure projects are appropriate for ages 11-20+.
  • Hardware: Projects should use hardware components readily available from UK suppliers (e.g., RS Components, The Pi Hut, Adafruit, Pimoroni, Kitronik).

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Additions welcome, particularly from teachers and club leaders with projects they've actually run with young people. A resource that survived contact with thirty teenagers is worth more than one that looks good in a search result.

docs.title: Inclusion criteria
docs.text:
Every entry must be:

  1. Free to access. No paywall, no mandatory account, no trial that expires. Freemium is acceptable only if the free tier is substantial enough to be useful alone (Random Nerd Tutorials qualifies; a site with three free articles does not).
  2. Buildable. Maps to components stocked by RS, The Pi Hut, Adafruit, Pimoroni or Kitronik — or runs in a free simulator.
  3. Currently live. Checked weekly by CI, but please verify before submitting.
  4. Age-appropriate for the stated band, including language, framing and safety practice.

We deliberately exclude paid courses even when they're excellent. There is more free material here than anyone can work through in a decade.

docs.title: Entry format
docs.text:
**[Resource name](https://example.com)** — `Difficulty` `Type`
One line on what it actually teaches. Parts: what you need to own.

Difficulty: Foundation (≈11–13) · Intermediate (≈14–16) · Advanced (≈17+) Tag where the resource starts, not where it ends.

Type: Video · Tutorial · Blog · GitHub · Curriculum · Simulator · Reference · Tool

docs.title: Writing style
docs.text:
• Say what it teaches, not that it's good. "Covers pull-up resistors and why floating inputs read noise" beats "great tutorial".
  • One line. Two if the resource needs a caveat.
  • Flag caveats honestly. If a channel has strong language, dangerous demonstrations, or a paywall behind the free tier, say so. Supervisors need this more than they need enthusiasm.
  • No affiliate links. Ever. This gets rejected on sight.
  • British English, since the buying guidance is UK-centred.

docs.title: How to submit
docs.text:
1. Open an issue using the Add a resource template, or
  2. Fork, add your entry to the right file, and open a pull request.

For a PR, please say in the description whether you've used the resource with learners, and roughly what ages.

docs.title: Reporting a broken or outdated link
docs.text:
Use the Broken link template. Automated checking catches dead URLs but not pages that are still live and now wrong — a discontinued product, a retired competition, a tutorial for hardware you can no longer buy. Those need human eyes, and reports are very welcome.

Time-sensitive pages that need periodic review: - docs/05-lego-2026-transition.md — a fast-moving situation - docs/03-buying-guide-uk.md — prices drift - competitions/ — seasons and rules change annually

docs.title: What gets rejected
docs.text:
• Paid courses, and freemium with a thin free tier
  • Affiliate or referral links
  • Products rather than learning resources
  • Anything requiring an account before you can see the content
  • Tutorials with unsafe practice — mains wiring aimed at under-18s, unprotected lithium charging, missing current limiting
  • AI-generated tutorial content that hasn't been verified against working hardware. Wiring diagrams that look plausible and aren't are actively harmful, and this is now a real problem in search results.

docs.title: Code of conduct
docs.text: This resource is aimed at children and young people. Contributors are expected to keep discussion constructive and appropriate to that audience. Disagreements about technical merit are fine and useful; anything else isn't.

docs.title: Competitions
docs.text:
A deadline and an audience change everything. Learners who drift on open-ended projects often transform when there's a date, a rulebook and other teams.

UK-focused, but most of these run internationally.

docs.title: Pi Wars — ages 11+ and adults
docs.text:
Raspberry Pi robots competing in non-destructive challenges, both autonomous and remote-controlled. Held over a weekend in Cambridge, with school, family, hobbyist and solo categories. Open to entrants worldwide. The YouTube channel has years of past runs, and competitor blogs are an excellent free build-log resource.

Why it's good: the challenge variety rewards different strengths, the community is unusually welcoming, and the barrier to a competitive entry is low. Probably the best first competition for a UK Pi-based team.

docs.title: FIRST LEGO League — ages 9–16
docs.text:
⚠️ The 2026–2027 BIOGLOW season is the final one. LEGO Education has not renewed its partnership with FIRST. Two editions run in parallel: Founders Edition on SPIKE hardware (final season 2027–2028) and Future Edition on the new Computer Science & AI kits. LEGO Education plans its own separate competition from 2027–2028.

Season materials — rubrics, scoresheets, judging flowcharts and twelve support sessions — are free to download and useful as a structure even outside the competition.

docs.title: VEX Robotics Competition — ages 8–18+
docs.text: VEX IQ (primary/lower secondary) and VEX V5 (upper secondary). Metal construction system, well-established, and now the strongest continuing option for schools leaving FLL. Runs through RoboticsEducation.org.

docs.title: FIRST Tech Challenge / FIRST Robotics Competition — ages 12–18
docs.text: Where FLL teams are now pointed. FRC in particular is a serious commitment — significant budget, a six-week build season, and a large mentor team — but the payoff is correspondingly large.

docs.title: RoboCup Junior — ages up to 19
docs.text: Soccer, rescue and OnStage leagues. Platform-agnostic, so a Pico or Arduino robot is entirely viable. Strong international pathway.

docs.title: Tomorrow's Engineers EEP Robotics Challenge — UK, ages 11–14
docs.text: Free to enter for UK schools, LEGO-based, and designed to need no prior robotics experience from the teacher. A good first step for a school with no existing programme.

docs.title: F1 in Schools — ages 9–19
docs.text: CAD, CFD, manufacturing, and a business case alongside the engineering. Broader than pure coding, and reaches learners who want the design and communication side.

docs.title: Formula Student — university level
docs.text: Where this pathway ends up. Worth showing to 16-year-olds as a destination.

docs.title: Astro Pi — ages up to 19, free
docs.text:
Write Python that runs on Raspberry Pi hardware aboard the ISS. Two tiers: Mission Zero takes a single lesson and every valid entry runs in space, which makes it the single highest-impact-per-hour activity in this entire repository. Mission Space Lab is a serious multi-month research project.

Run by the Raspberry Pi Foundation with ESA. Free. If you do one thing from this page, do Mission Zero.

docs.title: ESA CanSat — ages 14–19
docs.text: Build a satellite the size of a drinks can, launch it to ~1 km, recover and analyse the telemetry. National rounds including a UK competition, then a European final.

docs.title: UK Rocketry Challenge — ages 11–18
docs.text: Design, build and fly a rocket to a target altitude with a fragile payload.

docs.title: Coding (no hardware)
docs.text:
• Advent of Code — December daily puzzles, free, addictive, all languages
  • Bebras — UK computational thinking challenge, ages 6–18, free
  • UK Bebras → Oxford Computing Challenge → British Informatics Olympiad — the competitive programming pathway
  • Coolest Projects — Raspberry Pi Foundation showcase rather than a competition. No winners, no losers, any project accepted. Excellent for learners who freeze under competitive pressure.

docs.title: Choosing one
docs.text: If your group is… Try A school with no existing programme, no budget Astro Pi Mission Zero, then Bebras A school with LEGO already FLL Founders Edition while it lasts, then VEX IQ A hobbyist family or small club Pi Wars Ambitious 16–18s wanting a personal statement CanSat, Astro Pi Mission Space Lab, FRC Learners who dislike competition Coolest Projects

docs.title: Running a team: what actually helps
docs.text:
• Start earlier than feels necessary. Every experienced coach says this and every new coach ignores it.
  • Build two of everything critical. Robots break the week before. Spare motors and a spare controller cost less than a season.
  • Log everything. Photos, decisions, failed attempts. Most competitions score the engineering journal or judged presentation heavily, and it's the part teams leave until last. It's also the part that most resembles real engineering.
  • Let them lose properly. The learning is in the debrief. Coaches who build the robot produce teams who learned nothing and know it.
  • Watch past runs on YouTube. Pi Wars and FLL both have extensive archives. An hour of watching saves a month of guessing.

docs.title: For a parent
docs.text:
Start with the buying guide, pick Bundle A or B depending on age, then work through the "Start with" list in the matching track. Resist the urge to buy the exciting expensive thing first.

Your actual job during the first few months is mostly to sit nearby, resist solving the problem, and ask "what did you expect to happen?" when something doesn't work. That question does more than any tutorial.

docs.title: For a teacher or club leader
docs.text:
1. Free curricula has complete schemes of work — start there rather than assembling lessons from individual projects.
  2. Standardise on one platform. See buying guide § clubs.
  3. Read safety and adapt your risk assessment before the first hardware session.
  4. Use themes to find projects that fit a topic you're already teaching — a data-logging project drops neatly into a science scheme, a MIDI controller into music tech.

docs.title: For a learner working alone
docs.text:
Pick a theme you actually care about rather than a platform. Then find the cheapest board on that theme's page that does what you want, and follow one tutorial series to completion before jumping to another.

The most common failure mode is starting six projects and finishing none. Finish one bad project rather than starting three good ones.

docs.text: See CONTRIBUTING.md.

Type: Video · Tutorial · Blog · GitHub · Curriculum · Simulator · Reference

Where a resource spans levels, the tag shows where it starts.

docs.title: What qualifies for inclusion
docs.text:
Every entry must be:

  1. Free to access — no paywall, no mandatory account, no trial that expires.
  2. Buildable — maps to components stocked by a listed supplier, or runs in a free simulator.
  3. Currently live — checked automatically each week.
  4. Age-appropriate — suitable for the stated band, including language and safety framing.

Resources that are merely good but paid (Arduino's official courses, most Udemy content, CS50x certificates) are deliberately excluded. There's more than enough free material to fill a decade.

docs.title: Age bands & learning tracks
docs.text:
Ages 11 to 20+ is an enormous span — it covers a child who has never written a line of code and an undergraduate building a ROS 2 robot. Sorting purely by age fails, because readiness varies wildly. Sorting purely by difficulty fails too, because a 12-year-old and a 19-year-old need different framing for the same technical content.

So: three tracks, defined by what the learner can already do, with typical ages attached as a hint.

docs.title: Foundation — typically 11–13
docs.text:
Entry condition: can use a computer, has maybe done Scratch at school.

Exit condition: can write a 30-line MicroPython program, wire a sensor with crocodile clips, and debug by reading an error message.

Constraints that matter at this level: - No soldering. Use crocodile clips, Grove/STEMMA QT connectors, or edge connectors. - Immediate visible feedback. LEDs, sound, movement — something happens within 5 minutes. - Block coding first, text second. MakeCode's block↔Python toggle is the single best bridge that exists. - Projects finish in one sitting (45–90 min).

Best platforms: micro:bit v2, LEGO SPIKE Prime, Circuit Playground Express.

Start with: 1. micro:bit projects — official, free, filterable by difficulty 2. MakeCode for micro:bit — blocks with a JavaScript/Python toggle 3. Raspberry Pi Foundation Projects — filter to "Explore" 4. Adafruit Circuit Playground Express guides

Typical first five projects: step counter, reaction timer game, plant moisture alarm, micro:bit radio messaging between two boards, line-following buggy.

docs.title: Intermediate — typically 14–16
docs.text:
Entry condition: comfortable with variables, loops and functions. Willing to read documentation.

Exit condition: can breadboard a circuit from a schematic, solder a header, use I²C sensors, push code to GitHub, and Google an error productively.

What changes: - Text coding becomes the default (MicroPython / CircuitPython / Arduino C++). - Breadboards and jumper wires replace crocodile clips. First soldering happens here — see safety. - Projects span multiple sessions and need version control. - Datasheets enter the picture. Reading a sensor datasheet is a real skill. - Failure becomes normal and productive. This is the stage where debugging is genuinely learned.

Best platforms: Raspberry Pi Pico 2 / Pico 2 W, Adafruit Feather & QT Py, Arduino Uno/Nano, Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W.

Start with: 1. Raspberry Pi Pico Get Started guide — free, official 2. Adafruit Learning System — CircuitPython — the single best free electronics library on the internet 3. Paul McWhorter's Arduino series — genuinely structured lesson-by-lesson, homework included 4. Random Nerd Tutorials — enormous free ESP32/Pico project base

Typical projects: WiFi weather station logging to a dashboard, RC robot over Bluetooth, MIDI controller, e-ink dashboard, home security sensor, retro handheld game.

docs.title: Advanced — typically 17–20+
docs.text:
Entry condition: fluent in at least one language, comfortable on a command line, understands basic electronics (Ohm's law, pull-ups, current limiting).

Exit condition: portfolio-grade projects. University applications, apprenticeships, or genuinely useful hardware.

What changes: - Linux, SSH, systemd, cross-compilation. - C/C++ alongside Python — and understanding why you'd choose each. - PCB design (KiCad), 3D printing, CAD (Fusion, FreeCAD, OnShape). - ROS 2, computer vision, on-device machine learning. - Reading source code, contributing to open source, writing documentation.

Best platforms: Raspberry Pi 4/5, Pi Camera Module 3, ESP32, custom PCBs, LEGO hardware driven by Pybricks or ev3dev.

Start with: 1. Ben Eater — build a CPU from logic gates. Nothing else on the internet teaches computer architecture this well, and it's free. 2. ROS 2 official tutorials 3. Picamera2 manual & examples 4. KiCad official docs + Contextual Electronics free content 5. James Bruton / XRobots — advanced mechanical + electronics builds, fully open-sourced on GitHub

Typical projects: self-balancing robot, autonomous rover with SLAM, high-altitude balloon payload, custom PCB synthesiser, ML-based sorting machine, quadruped.

docs.title: Moving between tracks
docs.text:
The bridges matter more than the tracks themselves. Three specific transitions cause the most dropout:

Blocks → text. Don't jump. Use MakeCode's toggle to show the same program in both forms, repeatedly, for weeks. The realisation that they're the same thing is the whole point.

Crocodile clips → breadboard. The failure mode is invisible wiring errors. Teach a systematic check (power rails first, then ground, then signal) before it's needed, not after three hours of frustration.

One file → a project. Introduce Git before it's strictly necessary, on a project small enough that losing it wouldn't matter. Learning Git during a crisis is miserable.

docs.title: A note on "ages"
docs.text:
The bands above are guides. Two things override them:

  1. Prior exposure. A 13-year-old with two years of Code Club is intermediate. A 17-year-old starting cold is foundation — and will move through it in a fortnight rather than a year, which is fine.
  2. Support available. Foundation-level projects assume an adult nearby. Advanced projects assume the learner can unblock themselves. A well-supported 12-year-old can do intermediate work; an unsupported 16-year-old often can't.

Pitch to competence, not birthday.

docs.title: Buying guide (UK)
docs.text: What to buy, from where, and in what order. Written for parents, teachers and club leaders who want to spend once and spend well.

docs.title: The four suppliers, and what each is actually good for
The Pi Hut
docs.text: UK-based, next-day delivery, no import faff. The default choice for anything Raspberry Pi, Pico, micro:bit or Pimoroni. They stock Adafruit lines too, usually cheaper than importing directly once you account for duty. Their tutorial blog is free and well-written. Start here for most orders.

docs.title: RS Components
docs.text: Industrial supplier, so: enormous catalogue, proper datasheets, trade accounts, and reliable bulk pricing. Best for discrete components (resistor kits, capacitors, connectors), tools, and anything you need a hundred of. They're also an official Raspberry Pi distributor. Less hobbyist-friendly browsing — you need to know roughly what you want. Best for schools with purchase orders, and for component restocking.

docs.title: Adafruit
docs.text: US-based. The hardware is excellent and often unique (Circuit Playground, Feather, NeoPixels, STEMMA QT sensors), but the real value is the Learning System — thousands of free, well-produced guides, most under a Creative Commons licence. Shipping to the UK costs and takes time; check The Pi Hut or Pimoroni first for the same part. Buy the learning content for free, buy the hardware locally where you can.

docs.title: LEGO Education
docs.text:
See the LEGO transition page before spending anything here. SPIKE sales ended June 2026.

Worth adding: Pimoroni (Sheffield) and Kitronik (Nottingham). Both UK, both excellent, both publish free tutorials. Kitronik in particular writes classroom-ready micro:bit lesson material.

docs.title: Bundle A — Foundation, one learner (~£45)
docs.text:
Item Approx Why BBC micro:bit v2 £15 Accelerometer, mic, speaker, radio, all onboard Crocodile clip leads (10) £4 No soldering required Kitronik or Pi Hut micro:bit starter kit £20 LEDs, buzzer, servo, sensors Battery pack + AAA £5 Untethered projects matter more than you'd think

Gets you through roughly thirty projects before you need anything else.

docs.title: Bundle B — Intermediate, one learner (~£70)
docs.text: Item Approx Why Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W (with headers) £8 Dual-core, WiFi, MicroPython or C Half-size breadboard ×2 £6 One for the current project, one for the next Jumper wire assortment £6 Buy more than you think Component starter kit (resistors, LEDs, buttons, transistors) £18 RS is good value here Multimeter £15 Non-negotiable. Cheap is fine. Soldering iron (temperature-controlled) £25 See safety Assorted I²C sensors (STEMMA QT / Qwiic) £15 Plug-in sensors, no wiring errors

docs.title: Bundle C — Advanced, one learner (~£160)
docs.text: Raspberry Pi 5 (4GB) + official PSU + microSD + Camera Module 3 + motor driver HAT + chassis and motors. Add a 3D printer if the club has one; add KiCad and a cheap PCB fab run when they're ready.

docs.title: Bundle D — Classroom of 30 (~£700)
docs.text: 15× micro:bit v2 (pairs work better than solo), 15× accessory kits, a class set of crocodile leads, one teacher demo Raspberry Pi, and a consumables budget. Buy through RS on a PO. Budget 15% annually for replacement — things break, and that's fine.

docs.title: Buy-later, not buy-now
docs.text:
Common overspends, in rough order of regret:

  • Big robot kits before basics. A £200 kit that assembles in one afternoon and then sits on a shelf teaches less than £40 of loose parts.
  • A 3D printer, early. Useful eventually. A distraction at the start — you'll spend the term debugging the printer, not the robot.
  • Premium soldering stations. A £25 temperature-controlled iron is genuinely fine for years.
  • Discontinued LEGO at collector prices. See above.
  • Oscilloscopes. Real, but not before advanced track.

docs.title: Buy-first, no regrets
docs.text:
• A multimeter. Cheapest item on this list, highest diagnostic value.
  • More jumper wires than you need. They vanish.
  • A second board of whatever you're using. Halves debugging time — you can swap to isolate the fault.
  • Storage. A compartment box. Loose components in a drawer become no components.
  • Good side cutters and wire strippers. Bad ones make everything harder and are how people get hurt.

docs.title: Buying for a club or school
docs.text:
• Standardise. One platform, one version, across the whole group. Mixed hardware multiplies your support burden by more than you'd expect.
  • Pairs, not solos. Two learners per kit produces more discussion, more debugging and less passive following of instructions.
  • Consumables budget. Wires, batteries, solder, LEDs. Roughly 15% of hardware spend per year.
  • Check for grants. Raspberry Pi Foundation, IET, Tomorrow's Engineers and STEM Learning all run UK funding routes. Code Club provides free resources and training.
  • Simulate first. Wokwi and Tinkercad Circuits are free and let you validate a project plan before committing budget.

docs.title: Prices
docs.text: All figures are rough August 2026 UK retail, inclusive of VAT, and will drift. Treat them as ratios rather than quotes.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: Written for adults supervising young people. None of this is meant to be alarming — electronics at this level is a low-risk hobby. But a few specific things do cause real injuries, and they're worth knowing before rather than after.

docs.title: Soldering
docs.text:
Age: Typically from 12–13 with one-to-one supervision, and independently from around 14–15 depending on the individual.

  • Temperature-controlled iron, set around 350 °C. Cheap fixed-temperature irons run too hot and encourage bad technique.
  • Ventilation. Solder flux fumes are the actual respiratory hazard, not the metal. A window and a small fan pointing away from the work is enough. A fume extractor is better.
  • Lead-free solder for young people. It's slightly harder to work with. Do it anyway.
  • Wash hands after sessions, always, whichever solder you use. No food at the bench.
  • Iron goes back in the stand every single time. This is the habit that prevents burns, and it needs enforcing until it's automatic.
  • Safety glasses when trimming component legs. Snipped wire ends travel surprisingly fast.
  • Have burn first aid to hand: cool running water for 20 minutes. Know where the nearest tap is.

docs.title: Batteries
docs.text:
LiPo and lithium-ion cells are the highest-risk items most STEM clubs will handle. They store a lot of energy and fail energetically.

  • Never puncture, crush, or short a lithium cell.
  • Charge with a proper balance charger, on a non-flammable surface, while someone is present. Not overnight, not unattended.
  • A swollen, hot, or damaged cell is finished. Isolate it outdoors, away from anything flammable, and dispose of it at a proper recycling point.
  • For under-16s, prefer AA/AAA packs or USB power. The performance difference rarely matters for these projects and the risk difference is substantial.
  • Never connect batteries directly across a motor or LED without appropriate current limiting.

docs.title: Mains electricity
docs.text:
Simple rule for under-18s: nothing above 24 V, and nothing that plugs into a wall socket without a qualified adult doing the mains-side work.

That means no opening PSUs, no mains-powered relay projects, no rewiring lamps, no salvaging parts from mains appliances (capacitors in switch-mode supplies hold a dangerous charge long after unplugging). Home automation projects should switch mains loads via commercial smart plugs, never via a hand-built relay board on a breadboard.

Battery and USB-powered projects cover essentially everything in this repository.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
• Side cutters: point the offcut downward and away, or hold it. Safety glasses.
  • Drills and rotary tools: eye protection mandatory, tie back long hair, clamp the workpiece — never hold it in your other hand.
  • Hot glue: genuinely causes bad burns, and is often the least-supervised tool in the room. It's around 190 °C.
  • 3D printers: hot end and heated bed burn. Some filaments produce ultrafine particles — ventilate, and prefer PLA for enclosed classroom spaces.
  • Laser cutters: never operate unsupervised, never leave running unattended, and check the material is laser-safe (PVC releases chlorine gas — it is never acceptable to cut).

docs.title: Eyes and lasers
docs.text:
Any laser module above class 2 needs proper eye protection and adult control of the hardware. Laser diodes salvaged from DVD drives are a common project idea online and a genuinely bad one — they're high-power, uncollimated and invisible in the IR case. Don't.

Bright LEDs, particularly high-power white and UV, also warrant care. Don't stare into them, and don't point them at others.

docs.title: Online safety for IoT projects
docs.text:
Once a project connects to the internet, a new category of risk appears — and it's worth teaching explicitly, because it's the part that generalises to the rest of their life.

  • Never hard-code WiFi passwords or API keys into a file that gets pushed to GitHub. Teach .gitignore and a secrets.py pattern from day one. This is the single most common mistake and it's easy to prevent.
  • Don't port-forward a home router to expose a hobby project. Use a proper tunnelling service or keep it on the LAN.
  • Cameras: agree in advance where they point and who can see the feed. A camera project in a shared home needs a conversation with everyone in the house.
  • Anything publishing to a public dashboard should be assumed public forever.

docs.title: Supervision ratios
docs.text:
Rough guidance for clubs:

Activity Suggested ratio Block coding, no hardware 1:15 Crocodile clips, battery power 1:12 Breadboarding 1:10 Soldering 1:6, or 1:1 for first attempts LiPo charging, power tools 1:1, adult-operated

docs.title: Risk assessment
docs.text: UK schools and registered clubs will usually need a written risk assessment. STEM Learning and CLEAPSS publish templates and guidance for exactly this — CLEAPSS in particular is the standard reference for D&T and science practical safety in England and Wales, and member schools have free access.

docs.title: The LEGO robotics transition (2022–2028)
docs.text: Status as of August 2026. If you own LEGO robotics hardware, are about to buy some, or run a FIRST LEGO League team, the ground has shifted twice in four years. This page lays out what happened, what still works, and what to do.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
October 2022 — MINDSTORMS discontinued. LEGO retired the MINDSTORMS Robot Inventor set (51515) after 24 years of the MINDSTORMS line, redirecting the team elsewhere. LEGO Education SPIKE became the de facto successor.

June 2021 — MINDSTORMS Education EV3 retired, with the EV3 app and related support ending after 31 July 2026.

January 2026 — LEGO Education Computer Science & AI announced. A new K–8 (Years 1–9) classroom line, shipping from April 2026, starting around $339.95 per kit (roughly $85 per student across a group of four). It integrates motors and sensors into LEGO elements and introduces a browser-based "Coding Canvas" plus a Python package. Notably, it runs locally with no student login and no data collection.

30 June 2026 — SPIKE Prime and SPIKE Essential sales ended. The SPIKE App remains supported until 30 June 2031.

2026–2027 — FIRST LEGO League's final season. LEGO Education has not renewed its partnership with FIRST. The BIOGLOW season (kickoff 4 August 2026) is the last, running in two parallel editions: Founders Edition on SPIKE hardware, and Future Edition on the new Computer Science & AI kits. LEGO Education plans its own separate competition season from 2027–2028.

docs.title: If you already own SPIKE Prime, Robot Inventor or EV3
docs.text:
Your hardware is fine. Nothing stops working. The official app runs until 2031 for SPIKE, and the open-source community has you covered well beyond that.

The important move is to learn Pybricks — free, open-source MicroPython firmware that runs on SPIKE Prime, SPIKE Essential, MINDSTORMS Robot Inventor, EV3 and the Powered Up hubs. It replaces LEGO's app entirely with a browser-based Python environment at code.pybricks.com, works offline once loaded, and is developed independently of LEGO's support timeline.

Pybricks is genuinely better than the official software for anyone past block coding: proper Python, precise motor control, and support for third-party sensors. Flashing is reversible — you can restore LEGO firmware via the DFU bootloader.

Caveat: SPIKE Prime hubs manufactured in 2026 have different internal electronics and require different firmware. Pybricks support for those is in development, not yet shipped. Check the Pybricks support tracker before buying a brand-new hub secondhand.

docs.title: If you're buying now
docs.text:
Don't buy SPIKE Prime new at inflated prices. Discontinued kits tend to climb well above original retail, replacement parts are hard to source, and you're buying into a platform with a fixed end date.

Realistic options:

Option Why Cost Secondhand SPIKE Prime + Pybricks Best LEGO experience, open-source software future, still FLL-legal for Founders Edition through 2027–28 Variable, watch for inflation Secondhand EV3 + Pybricks Cheap, robust, huge community, now flashable over USB in seconds Low LEGO Education Computer Science & AI The supported path forward, and the basis of FLL Future Edition ~$340/kit, classroom-oriented Move off LEGO entirely micro:bit or Pi Pico robotics gives more transferable skills for less money £15–60

docs.title: If you run an FLL team
docs.text: Founders Edition (SPIKE-based) runs through the 2027–2028 season, so existing hardware has at least two more seasons. Future Edition needs the new CS & AI kits. Regional availability varies — check with your local partner before committing budget. After 2027–28, LEGO Education runs its own competition and FIRST teams are pointed toward FIRST Tech Challenge and FIRST Robotics Competition.

docs.title: The honest assessment
docs.text:
LEGO robotics has always traded openness for polish. You get an excellent building system and a friendly app, in exchange for a closed ecosystem whose lifespan is decided by a toy company's strategy. That trade just came due for the second time in four years.

For an 11–13-year-old who loves building, SPIKE Prime with Pybricks is still a superb experience and the block-to-Python path is well-trodden. For a 14+ learner, the money goes considerably further on a Pi Pico, a motor driver and a chassis — and the skills transfer to everything else in this repository.

docs.title: Free LEGO robotics resources that remain live
docs.text:
• Pybricks documentation — getting started, API reference, tutorials. Intermediate
  • pybricks/pybricks-projects — a broad collection of example programs and robot builds. Intermediate GitHub
  • Anton's Mindstorms — the best independent LEGO robotics blog; Python-first, active through 2026. Intermediate Advanced
  • ev3dev — Debian Linux on the EV3 brick, with Python, C++ and more. Advanced GitHub
  • FIRST LEGO League season materials — rubrics, scoresheets and session slides, free to download. Curriculum
  • LEGO Education lesson plans — free, still hosted, still useful even for retired kits. Curriculum

See also: platforms/lego-robotics.md.

This page is time-sensitive. If you're reading it well after August 2026, verify against education.lego.com and firstlegoleague.org — and please open an issue if it's out of date.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text:
Resources grouped by hardware family. If you already own something, start with its page. If you're choosing, use the comparison below then read the buying guide.

Platform Ages Entry cost Soldering Ceiling BBC micro:bit v2 11–14 ~£15 No Low Raspberry Pi Pico / Pico 2 13+ ~£5 Headers Very high ESP32 & M5Stack 13+ ~£15–40 No (M5Stack) Very high Raspberry Pi (Zero 2 W / 4 / 5) 14+ ~£18–80 No Very high Arduino & Adafruit 13+ ~£10–30 Some High LEGO robotics ⚠️ 11–16 £££ No Medium VEX Robotics & VEXcode VR 11–18 £0–£££ No High Programmable Drones 13+ ~£100 No High AI & Machine Vision 13+ ~£45–100 No High Electronics fundamentals All ~£25 Eventually Unlimited

⚠️ LEGO Education ended SPIKE sales in June 2026 — read this before buying.

docs.title: Choosing, briefly
docs.text:
Never touched hardware? micro:bit. The onboard sensors mean your first ten projects need nothing else, which removes wiring errors from the equation entirely.

Comfortable with code, want to build things? Pico 2 W. Five to seven pounds for a dual-core WiFi microcontroller with excellent documentation is unmatched.

Want cameras, vision, AI, or a web server? Raspberry Pi. It's the only option here that runs Linux.

Following a specific tutorial? Use whatever it uses. Fighting a substitution while also learning is two problems at once.

Want to make wearables or soft circuits? Adafruit — Circuit Playground and the Flora range, plus Becky Stern's guides.

No budget yet? Wokwi and Tinkercad Circuits simulate most of this for free in a browser.

docs.title: A common mistake
docs.text:
Picking the platform before picking the project. A learner who wants to make a light-up jacket and gets handed a Raspberry Pi will lose interest, and a learner who wants to do face recognition on a micro:bit will hit a wall.

Start from themes — what do they actually want to make? — and let that choose the board.

docs.title: AI & Machine Vision
docs.text:
Best for: ages 13+, facial recognition, object tracking, edge machine learning Cost: ~£45 (HuskyLens) to £100+ (Raspberry Pi AI kit) Languages: Python · MakeCode Blocks Buy: The Pi Hut · Pimoroni

Artificial Intelligence and machine vision can seem completely out of reach for a 12-year-old on a £15 micro:bit. However, "Edge AI" modules have changed this. Instead of a microcontroller trying to process heavy video feeds, dedicated AI cameras process the video locally and simply send the results (e.g., "I see a face at X,Y coordinates") to the microcontroller over simple wires.

docs.title: DFRobot HuskyLens (No-Code/Low-Code AI)
docs.text:
HuskyLens Official Wiki — Foundation Intermediate Reference HuskyLens is an easy-to-use AI machine vision sensor with a built-in screen. It can learn to recognize faces, track colors, and read QR codes with the press of a single button. Parts needed: HuskyLens, micro:bit or Arduino.

MakeCode Extension for HuskyLens — Foundation GitHub Use block coding to make your micro:bit robot react to what the HuskyLens sees. Parts needed: micro:bit, HuskyLens, robotics chassis.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi AI Kit (Advanced Neural Networks)
docs.text: Raspberry Pi AI Kit Documentation — Advanced Reference For older students, the Hailo-8L M.2 accelerator combined with a Raspberry Pi 5 allows running full real-time neural networks (like object detection and pose estimation) in Python at 30+ frames per second. Parts needed: Raspberry Pi 5, AI Kit, Pi Camera.

docs.title: Project ideas by track
docs.text:
Foundation ideas (HuskyLens + micro:bit): an interactive pet robot that only follows its owner's face · a smart barrier that opens only when it reads an authorized QR code

Intermediate ideas (HuskyLens + Arduino): an automated turret that tracks specific colored objects · a line-following robot that recognizes intersections and street signs

Advanced ideas (Raspberry Pi + AI Kit): real-time traffic monitoring camera that counts cars vs bicycles · posture correction monitor that tracks human skeletal joints in real time

docs.title: Arduino & Adafruit
docs.text:
Best for: ages 13+, wearables, the deepest tutorial library anywhere Cost: ~£10–30 per board Languages: CircuitPython · Arduino C++ · MicroPython Buy: Adafruit (US) · The Pi Hut (UK stockist) · Pimoroni · RS

Two ecosystems, treated together because they overlap heavily in practice.

Arduino is the older, larger world: an enormous body of tutorials, shields and community code, built around C++. If a project exists anywhere on the internet, an Arduino version of it probably exists.

Adafruit makes distinctive hardware — Circuit Playground, Feather, QT Py, NeoPixels, STEMMA QT sensors — but its real contribution to education is learn.adafruit.com, which is very likely the single largest collection of free, well-produced electronics tutorials in existence. Most of it is Creative Commons licensed, meaning teachers can legally adapt it.

docs.title: Official & free
docs.text:
Adafruit Learning System — Foundation Intermediate Advanced Tutorial Thousands of guides, each with parts list, wiring diagram, full code and photos. Filterable by category and difficulty. Genuinely exceptional. Bookmark it. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Welcome to CircuitPython — Intermediate Tutorial The canonical starting guide. CircuitPython's model — the board mounts as a USB drive, you edit code.py, it reruns instantly — removes the whole compile-upload cycle. For beginners this is a significant advantage over Arduino C++. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

circuitpython.org — Reference Downloads, supported boards, and the library bundle. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Circuit Playground Express guides — Foundation Tutorial Sensors, LEDs, speaker and accelerometer all onboard, alligator-clip pads, and MakeCode block support. The closest Adafruit equivalent to a micro:bit, and an excellent classroom board. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Arduino Docs — Intermediate Reference Official language reference and board documentation. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Arduino Project Hub — Foundation Intermediate Tutorial Community projects with code and wiring. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Tinkercad Circuits — Foundation Simulator Free browser simulation of Arduino plus components, with block coding available. Superb for classrooms with more students than boards. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Wokwi — Intermediate Simulator More capable simulation covering Arduino, ESP32 and Pico. Free, no install. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.text:

docs.title: Project ideas by track
docs.text:
Foundation: Circuit Playground light-reactive NeoPixel patterns · sound-triggered effects · shake-to-roll dice · capacitive touch instrument

Intermediate: LED sneakers or a light-up costume (Becky Stern's guides) · plant monitor posting to a phone · IR remote-controlled robot · ESP32 WiFi weather display · MIDI foot controller · door sensor with notification

Advanced: LoRa long-range sensor network · CircuitPython driver written from a datasheet for an unsupported sensor · custom Feather-format PCB in KiCad · on-device ML with Edge Impulse (free developer tier) · quadruped with inverse kinematics

docs.title: Practical notes for UK buyers
docs.text:
Adafruit ships from the US. Once postage and duty are counted, check The Pi Hut and Pimoroni first — both stock much of the Adafruit range domestically. The tutorials are free regardless of where you buy the parts, and most work fine with generic equivalents.

STEMMA QT / Qwiic connectors are worth seeking out for classroom use specifically. They're keyed I²C plugs, so sensors physically cannot be miswired. This eliminates the single most common cause of "it doesn't work and we don't know why".

docs.title: Programmable Drones & Flight
docs.text:
Best for: ages 13+, robotics in 3D space, Python scripting, aerospace enthusiasts Cost: ~£100 (DJI Tello EDU) Languages: Python · Scratch (Blocks) Buy: DJI Store · The Pi Hut

Moving from wheeled rovers to flying robots introduces students to aerodynamics, 3D coordinates, and real-world control systems.

While building a custom drone from scratch requires advanced soldering and PID tuning (often reserved for university students), the DJI Tello EDU has become the standard for school drone programming. It allows students to write Python scripts to control a pre-built drone autonomously.

docs.title: Tello EDU (Python Drone Programming)
docs.text:
DJITelloPy Library — Intermediate Advanced GitHub The open-source Python library for controlling the Tello. Includes easy-to-read examples for taking off, flipping, and capturing video streams. Parts needed: Tello EDU drone, Wi-Fi enabled computer.

Tello EDU Official Blocks — Foundation Simulator Software to program the drone using Scratch-style blocks. Parts needed: Tello EDU drone.

DroneBlocks — Foundation Intermediate Curriculum An extensive curriculum dedicated to programming drones in education, featuring both block coding and Python courses. Parts needed: Tello EDU drone.

docs.title: High-Altitude & Space Projects
docs.text: ESA CanSat Student Training Academy — Intermediate Advanced Curriculum European Space Agency guides for designing, coding, and launching a soda-can-sized satellite payload with atmospheric telemetry. Parts needed: Arduino/microcontroller, sensors, radio transceiver.

docs.title: Project ideas by track
docs.text:
Tello Swarm (Python) — Advanced Tutorial Use Python threading and multiple Wi-Fi adapters to command a synchronized swarm of drones. Parts needed: Multiple Tello EDU drones.

Foundation ideas (Blocks): simple take-off and land · fly in a square · flip over obstacles

Intermediate ideas (Python): fly autonomously through a physical hoop course using pre-programmed coordinates · trigger drone commands using keyboard inputs on a laptop

Advanced ideas (Python + OpenCV): stream live video from the drone to a computer · program the drone to recognize and follow a human face autonomously

docs.title: Electronics fundamentals
docs.text:
Best for: everyone, at every stage Cost: ~£25 for a decent component kit, ~£15 for a multimeter Buy: RS for components in bulk · The Pi Hut for starter kits

This is the layer underneath every other page. A learner who understands why a resistor goes in series with an LED will debug their own problems for the next decade. One who doesn't will keep destroying components and not know why.

It's also the layer most often skipped, because blinking an LED via a library feels like progress and Ohm's law feels like homework. Worth resisting.

docs.title: The concepts that actually matter
docs.text:
In rough order of how often not knowing them causes a project to fail:

  1. Voltage, current, resistance and how they relate. Ohm's law, genuinely used, not memorised.
  2. Current limiting. Why an LED needs a resistor, and how to pick the value.
  3. Pull-up and pull-down resistors. Why a floating input reads garbage.
  4. Logic levels. 3.3 V vs 5 V, and why mixing them destroys boards.
  5. Current capacity. Why a GPIO pin can't drive a motor, and what a transistor or driver IC is for.
  6. Decoupling capacitors. Why circuits work on a bench and fail with a motor attached.
  7. Common ground. The single most common wiring error in multi-board projects.

docs.title: Free courses & tutorials
docs.text:
SparkFun Learn — Concepts — Foundation Intermediate Tutorial The best free written explanations of fundamentals, with genuinely good diagrams. Their voltage/current/resistance, pull-up resistor, and logic level tutorials are worth using directly as lesson material. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

All About Circuits — Textbooks — Intermediate Advanced Reference A complete, free, multi-volume electronics textbook. Dense but authoritative — the reference for when a question goes deeper than a tutorial covers. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Khan Academy — Electrical Engineering — Intermediate Curriculum Free, structured, with exercises. Good for the maths-adjacent learner. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Adafruit Learn — Electronics basics — Foundation Tutorial

CircuitLab / Falstad circuit simulator — Intermediate Simulator Falstad's free browser simulator animates current flow through a circuit. Seeing charge move makes several concepts click that text never does. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.title: Video
docs.text:
Ben Eater — Advanced Video Builds a working 8-bit computer on breadboards from logic gates, then a 6502 machine, explaining every step. There is nothing else like it at any price. Also covers networking from first principles. Companion kits and free written material at eater.net. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

GreatScott! — Intermediate Video Short, dense component explainers. Excellent on transistors, MOSFETs, boost converters. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

ElectroBOOM — Intermediate Video Mehdi Sadaghdar teaches real electronics theory through deliberately painful demonstrations. Very effective and very memorable. Note for supervisors: he intentionally does dangerous things with mains and high voltage for comedy, which he flags but which younger viewers may not parse. Pair with an explicit conversation about what not to copy. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Afrotechmods — Intermediate Video Short, clear, no-nonsense component tutorials. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

EEVblog — Advanced Video Dave Jones on test equipment, teardowns and design. The multimeter tutorials are the standard reference. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.title: Tools & design software (all free)
docs.text:
KiCad — Advanced Tool Full open-source PCB design. Schematic capture through to Gerber output. Official docs are thorough, and Contextual Electronics publishes free tutorial series. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Fritzing — Foundation Tool Breadboard-style diagrams. Source is free; binaries carry a small fee. Best for documenting wiring for others rather than for real design. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Falstad Circuit Simulator — Intermediate Simulator

Wokwi — Intermediate Simulator Simulates microcontrollers with their circuits — the bridge between electronics theory and embedded code. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

FreeCAD / OnShape free tier — Advanced Tool For enclosures, brackets and mechanical parts. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
kitspace/awesome-electronics — GitHub Curated index of resources, tools, and reference material. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Digital Electronics / nand2tetris — Advanced Curriculum Build a computer from NAND gates up to an operating system. Free course materials, and the first half runs entirely in simulation — no hardware needed. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.title: A minimum viable component kit
docs.text:
For a learner or small club, roughly £30 at RS:

  • Resistor assortment (E12 values, ¼ W) — you will use 220 Ω, 1 kΩ and 10 kΩ constantly
  • LEDs, assorted colours, 5 mm
  • Tactile push buttons
  • 2N2222 and BC547 transistors, a few logic-level MOSFETs
  • 1N4148 and 1N4007 diodes
  • Ceramic capacitors (100 nF especially) and a few electrolytics
  • Potentiometers, 10 kΩ
  • LDR, thermistor, piezo buzzer
  • Half-size breadboards ×2 and jumper wires
  • A multimeter — the highest-value item on the list

docs.title: Teaching sequence that works
docs.text:
1. LED and resistor. Calculate the resistor rather than being given it. Get it wrong deliberately once (too large — dim, not destroyed) to see the relationship.
  2. Button with a pull-up. Then remove the pull-up and watch the input read noise. The failure teaches more than the success.
  3. Transistor switching an LED, then a motor. Introduces "the microcontroller can't do this directly".
  4. Voltage divider with an LDR. Connects to analogue reading.
  5. Motor with a driver IC and a flyback diode. Introduces inductive kickback and why circuits fail intermittently.
  6. Measure everything with the multimeter at every step. The habit of measuring rather than guessing is the actual lesson.

docs.title: ESP32 & M5Stack Ecosystem
docs.text:
Best for: ages 13+, IoT, wearables, screen-based physical computing, no-soldering options Cost: ~£5 for bare ESP32, ~£15–40 for M5Stack devices Languages: MicroPython · Arduino C++ · UIFlow (Blocks) Buy: The Pi Hut · Pimoroni · RS

The ESP32 is the industry standard for low-cost Wi-Fi and Bluetooth microcontrollers. It powers countless commercial smart home devices.

While bare ESP32 boards (like the NodeMCU or WROOM) are fantastic for intermediate learners on breadboards, M5Stack has revolutionized the ESP32 for education. They wrap the ESP32 in robust plastic cases, add built-in screens, batteries, and buttons, and use plug-and-play Grove connectors. This completely eliminates fragile wiring for younger learners while retaining the full power of the ESP32.

docs.title: M5Stack (Zero-Wiring ESP32)
docs.text:
M5Stack Official Documentation — Foundation Intermediate Reference The central hub for pinouts, tutorials, and quick-start guides for the M5Core, M5StickC Plus, and ATOM series. Parts needed: M5Stack device.

UIFlow Web IDE — Foundation Simulator M5Stack's browser-based block programming environment that can instantly push code over Wi-Fi to a device without USB cables. Parts needed: M5Stack device.

Random Nerd Tutorials: M5Stack Guide — Intermediate Tutorial Step-by-step guides for programming the M5Stack core using the Arduino IDE, covering Wi-Fi servers and sensor displays. Parts needed: M5Stack Core.

docs.title: Bare ESP32 (Breadboarding & IoT)
docs.text:
Getting Started with ESP32 (Random Nerd Tutorials) — Intermediate Tutorial The internet's most comprehensive free guide to building Wi-Fi web servers, weather stations, and Bluetooth beacons with an ESP32. Parts needed: ESP32 board, breadboard, LEDs.

MicroPython on ESP32 Docs — Intermediate Advanced Reference Official quick reference for writing MicroPython on the ESP32, covering networking, deep sleep, and hardware interrupts. Parts needed: ESP32 board.

docs.title: Project ideas by track
docs.text:
ESP32 Web Server (Arduino IDE) — Intermediate Tutorial Build a standalone web server to control outputs (like LEDs or relays) from a smartphone browser over Wi-Fi. Parts needed: ESP32, breadboard, LED.

M5StickC Plus Environment Monitor — Foundation Tutorial Use UIFlow blocks to read an ENV III sensor unit and display real-time temperature and humidity on the built-in LCD screen. Parts needed: M5StickC Plus, ENV unit.

Foundation ideas (M5Stack): smart stopwatch · Wi-Fi message board · Pomodoro timer · tilt-controlled screen game

Intermediate ideas (ESP32): DHT11 weather station posting to a web dashboard · Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacon · internet radio player · home automation relay controller

Advanced ideas: OTA (Over-The-Air) firmware updates · ESP-NOW mesh networking between multiple robots · camera streaming (ESP32-CAM)

docs.title: LEGO robotics (SPIKE / MINDSTORMS / Pybricks)
docs.text:
Best for: ages 11–16, no soldering, competitions, learners who build before they code Cost: high, and now complicated — read the transition page first Languages: LEGO block editors · Python (via SPIKE app or Pybricks) · MicroPython (Pybricks)

⚠️ Status, August 2026. MINDSTORMS was discontinued in 2022. LEGO Education ended SPIKE Prime and SPIKE Essential sales on 30 June 2026, with app support continuing to 2031. The successor is LEGO Education Computer Science & AI (shipping since April 2026). FIRST LEGO League runs its final season in 2026–2027. Full detail: docs/05-lego-2026-transition.md.

Despite all that, existing LEGO hardware remains genuinely excellent for teaching, and the open-source community has made it independent of LEGO's roadmap. If you already own a set, this page is for you.

docs.title: Pybricks — the open-source route
docs.text:
Pybricks is free MicroPython firmware for LEGO hubs: SPIKE Prime, SPIKE Essential, MINDSTORMS Robot Inventor, EV3, and the Powered Up range. It replaces the official app with a browser IDE at code.pybricks.com that works offline once loaded.

Why it matters: it's real Python with precise motor control and third-party sensor support, it's developed independently of LEGO, and it keeps hardware useful long after official support ends. Flashing is reversible via the DFU bootloader.

Pybricks documentation — Intermediate Tutorial Getting started, tutorials, full API reference. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

pybricks/pybricks-projects — Intermediate GitHub Example programs and complete robot builds across every supported hub. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

pybricks/pybricks-micropython — Advanced GitHub The firmware source. Well-structured, actively maintained, and a plausible first contribution target. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Pybricks support tracker — Reference Check here before buying new hardware — SPIKE Prime hubs made in 2026 use different internals and firmware support is still in development. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.title: ev3dev — Linux on the EV3
docs.text:
ev3dev.org — Advanced Tutorial A Debian-based OS that boots on the EV3 brick from an SD card. Python, C++, Node.js, and a real Linux environment on a robot. For a sixth-former with a hand-me-down EV3, this is a superb and very cheap route into embedded Linux. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

ev3dev/ev3dev — Advanced GitHub

docs.text:
LEGO Education lesson plans — Foundation Curriculum Free, curriculum-mapped lessons. Still hosted for retired kits. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.title: The honest assessment
docs.text:
LEGO's strength is that the building is genuinely excellent and the barrier to a working robot is close to zero — no soldering, no wiring errors, no burned-out components. For an 11–13-year-old, that's exactly right, and the block-to-Python path through Pybricks is well-trodden.

Its weakness is cost and closure. A SPIKE Prime set costs roughly ten times a Pico-based robot with comparable capability, and the platform's lifespan is decided by a toy company. That has now ended twice in four years.

Practical recommendation: if you own it, keep it and learn Pybricks. If you're starting from nothing with a budget, put the money into Pico or micro:bit robotics and spend the difference on more learners.

docs.title: BBC micro:bit v2
docs.text:
Best for: ages 11–14, classrooms, first hardware, no soldering Cost: ~£15 board, ~£35 with a starter kit Languages: MakeCode blocks → JavaScript → MicroPython Buy: The Pi Hut · Kitronik · RS · Pimoroni

The v2 board has an accelerometer, compass, temperature sensor, microphone, speaker, touch logo, 25-LED display, radio and Bluetooth built in. That matters enormously for beginners: your first ten projects need no extra components at all, which removes the entire category of wiring-error frustration from the learning curve.

Its other superpower is the MakeCode block↔Python toggle. The same program, viewed two ways, on demand. Nothing else bridges that gap as cleanly.

docs.title: Honest limitations
docs.text:
• Limited RAM and no filesystem to speak of. Data logging is possible but cramped.
  • The edge connector needs a breakout board for anything beyond crocodile clips, which is an extra purchase and a small conceptual hurdle.
  • Learners outgrow it, usually around 14. That's a feature, not a bug — it's designed as an on-ramp. Plan the transition to Pico rather than trying to stretch the micro:bit past its useful range.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi Pico / Pico 2
docs.text:
Best for: ages 13+, the best price-to-capability ratio in this entire collection Cost: ~£4 (Pico 2) to ~£7 (Pico 2 W with WiFi) Languages: MicroPython · CircuitPython · C/C++ · Rust Buy: The Pi Hut · Pimoroni · RS

Two generations exist. The original Pico uses the RP2040; Pico 2 uses the RP2350, with faster cores, double the SRAM and flash, and a genuinely unusual party trick — you can choose between dual Arm Cortex-M33 cores or dual open-hardware Hazard3 RISC-V cores on the same chip. The W variants add WiFi and Bluetooth 5.2.

For a learner moving off blocks, this is the board to buy. Seven pounds for a WiFi-capable dual-core microcontroller with first-class documentation is not a deal that existed a decade ago.

docs.text:
Best for: ages 14+, Linux, cameras, computer vision, anything needing a real operating system Cost: ~£18 (Zero 2 W) to ~£80 (Pi 5, 4GB) Languages: Python · C/C++ · JavaScript · anything Linux runs Buy: The Pi Hut · RS · Pimoroni

The crucial distinction from the Pico: this is a computer, not a microcontroller. It boots Linux, runs a browser, hosts a web server, and drives a camera at 4K. That opens up computer vision, machine learning, networking and web development — none of which a microcontroller can touch.

The trade-off is boot time, power draw, SD card corruption, and the need to shut down gracefully. For blinking an LED, use a Pico. For recognising a face, use a Pi.

docs.title: Which Pi to buy
docs.text:
Board Use it for Avoid it for Zero 2 W (~£18) Embedded projects, wearables, robot brains where size matters Desktop use, heavy vision work Pi 4 (~£45+) The reliable middle. Plenty for most projects. Nothing much — still excellent Pi 5 (~£60+) Camera work, ML inference, anything CPU-heavy Battery projects — it draws real power Pi 500 / 400 Classroom desktops, a computer that lives in a keyboard GPIO-heavy projects (awkward access)

Add: a good power supply (most mysterious Pi problems are undervoltage), a decent A2-rated microSD card or an SSD for the Pi 5, and active cooling for the Pi 5.

docs.title: Things that will bite you
docs.text:
• SD card corruption from pulling the power. Teach sudo shutdown now as a ritual, and consider read-only root for kiosk projects.
  • Undervoltage. A phone charger is not a Pi power supply. The rainbow square and inexplicable crashes are almost always this.
  • GPIO is 3.3 V, not 5 V. Connecting a 5 V signal to a GPIO pin destroys it. Worth teaching level shifting before it costs someone a board.
  • No analogue inputs. Unlike a Pico or Arduino, the Pi has no ADC. You need an external one (MCP3008) or a companion microcontroller.

docs.title: Reference documentation worth teaching learners to read
docs.text:
Getting a 15-year-old comfortable with primary documentation is one of the highest-leverage things you can do. These are the friendliest starting points:

  • gpiozero recipes — documentation that reads like a project list
  • MicroPython docs — clear, well-organised
  • micro:bit MicroPython docs — deliberately beginner-oriented
  • Raspberry Pi documentation — CC BY-SA, so reusable in your own materials
  • CircuitPython libraries — consistent structure across hundreds of drivers

The skill to build is scanning — finding the one function you need without reading the page. Model it out loud a few times and most learners pick it up quickly.

Ben Eater’s 8-Bit Computer — Advanced Video Build a fully working 8-bit computer on breadboards from basic TTL logic gates, learning computer architecture, ALU design, and machine code. Parts needed: Breadboards, 7400-series logic chips, EEPROM.

Introduction to TinyML (Harvard / tinyml.seas.harvard.edu) — Advanced Curriculum Free educational resources and lectures on deploying machine learning models to ultra-low-power microcontrollers. Parts needed: Arduino Nano 33 BLE or Raspberry Pi Pico.

ROS 2 Official Tutorials — Advanced Tutorial Progressive guide from the Open Source Robotics Foundation on nodes, topics, services, actions, and creating full autonomous robot software stacks. Parts needed: Linux computer or Raspberry Pi 4/5.

ESA CanSat Training Academy — Intermediate Advanced Curriculum European Space Agency guides for designing, coding, and launching a soda-can-sized satellite payload with atmospheric telemetry. Parts needed: Microcontroller, sensors, radio transceiver.

nand2tetris — Advanced Curriculum Build a computer from NAND gates up through a CPU, assembler, compiler and operating system. Free course materials; the first half runs entirely in simulation. Parts needed: Computer with internet access.

Khan Academy — Computing — Foundation Intermediate Curriculum Free, structured, with automatic exercises. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Carnegie Mellon Robotics Academy — Intermediate Curriculum Robotics curricula with a meaningful free tier and strong computational-thinking framing. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.title: Assembling your own scheme of work
docs.text:
If none of the above quite fits, the pattern that works over a school year:

Term 1 — Foundation, no soldering. micro:bit, block coding moving to Python via the MakeCode toggle. One finished project per fortnight. The goal is confidence and the habit of finishing.

Term 2 — Breadboarding and sensors. Move to Pico or keep micro:bit with a breakout. Introduce the multimeter, Ohm's law, pull-up resistors. Projects span two to three sessions. Introduce Git here, on something small.

Term 3 — An open project. Learners choose. They will pick something too ambitious; let them, then help them scope it down in week two rather than week eight. End with a showcase — an audience does more for quality than any amount of marking.

Three principles that matter more than the content:

  • Finish things. A completed simple project beats an abandoned impressive one, every time. This is the single biggest predictor of whether a learner continues.
  • Pairs, not solos. Two per kit produces discussion, debugging and explanation. One per kit produces silent instruction-following.
  • Let the failures happen. A circuit that doesn't work is the lesson. Rescuing too early removes the entire learning opportunity — and learners can tell when they've been rescued.

docs.title: Teaching Git alongside the projects
docs.text:
Version control is the skill most likely to transfer directly into employment, and it's easiest to teach when the stakes are low.

Introduce it early, on something disposable. Learning Git during a crisis — after losing work, under deadline — is miserable and sticks badly.

A workable sequence:

  1. git init, add, commit on a single-file project. Nothing else. Just build the save habit.
  2. git log and git diff — the moment they see their own history is the moment it makes sense.
  3. Push to GitHub. A public portfolio starting at 14 is worth a great deal by 18.
  4. Branching when they first want to try something risky without breaking what works.
  5. Pull requests — ideally against a classmate's repo before attempting a real open-source contribution.

Teach .gitignore and secrets handling from day one. Committing WiFi passwords and API keys to a public repo is the single most common and most consequential beginner mistake. A secrets.py in .gitignore, established as a reflex before it matters, prevents it permanently.

A realistic first contribution: documentation fixes and typo corrections in the repos above. Both CircuitPython and MicroPython maintainers are welcoming to first-timers, and having a merged PR at 16 is genuinely notable on a university or apprenticeship application.

docs.title: Video channels
docs.text: Free YouTube channels worth following, with the good starting point flagged for each. All active as of August 2026.

docs.title: Structured courses (start here for self-directed learners)
docs.text:
Paul McWhorter — Intermediate Numbered lesson series with homework at the end of each video, for Arduino, Raspberry Pi and Python. This is the closest thing on YouTube to an actual course, and it's the best free option for a motivated teenager working alone. Start with lesson 1 of the Arduino series and don't skip. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Kevin McAleer / kevsrobots — Intermediate Pico robotics, prolific and UK-based. Everything is open-sourced, and kevsrobots.com has free written courses alongside. Best single channel for Pico-based robots. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Core Electronics — Foundation Intermediate Clear, well-produced, spanning micro:bit, Pico and Pi. Strong on explaining why. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.title: Electronics theory
docs.text:
Ben Eater — Advanced Builds an 8-bit computer from logic gates on breadboards, then a 6502 machine, explaining every decision. Also networking from first principles. There is genuinely nothing comparable at any price. Free written material at eater.net. Start with the 8-bit computer playlist. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

GreatScott! — Intermediate Short, dense component explainers. Excellent on transistors, MOSFETs and power supplies. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

Afrotechmods — Intermediate No-nonsense component tutorials, short and clear. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

EEVblog — Advanced Dave Jones on test gear, teardowns and design practice. His multimeter tutorials are the standard reference. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

ElectroBOOM — Intermediate Real theory delivered through deliberately painful demonstrations. Memorable and effective. Supervisor note: he intentionally does dangerous things with mains for comedy. He flags this; younger viewers may not register it. Worth an explicit conversation — see safety. Parts needed: See tutorial for details.

docs.text:

docs.title: Using video well
docs.text:
Video is the worst medium for reference and one of the best for motivation. The pattern that works:

  1. Watch a project video to decide you want to build it.
  2. Switch to written instructions to actually build it — you can't scrub a video with solder in your hand.
  3. Return to video for the bits where seeing the physical technique matters (soldering, mechanical assembly).

Channels that publish written companions — DroneBot Workshop, Kevin McAleer, Ben Eater — are worth more than their view counts suggest for exactly this reason.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: Same resources, sliced by what the learner actually wants to make. This is usually the better entry point — motivation picks the project, and the project picks the hardware.

docs.title: 🤖 Robots & rovers
docs.text:
The default STEM project, and for good reason: movement is immediately legible as success or failure.

  • Kevin McAleer's robot builds — Intermediate Tutorial — free written courses plus video, all open-sourced. Pico-based. The best free robotics curriculum for this age range.
  • Raspberry Pi Foundation — Build a robot buggy — Foundation Tutorial
  • Pybricks projects — Intermediate GitHub — LEGO robots in real Python
  • DroneBot Workshop — motors and drivers — Intermediate Video — the theory most robot tutorials skip
  • James Bruton / XRobots — Advanced Video — self-balancing, quadrupeds, mechanum drives; everything on GitHub
  • ROS 2 tutorials — Advanced Tutorial — the professional robotics framework

Progression: line follower → obstacle avoidance → PID control → odometry → SLAM. PID line-following is the sweet spot around 14–16: real control theory, visible results, achievable in a term.

docs.title: 👕 Wearables & e-textiles
docs.text:
Reaches learners who bounce off robots entirely. Also the theme with the best gender balance in most clubs, which is worth knowing when planning.

  • Becky Stern — Intermediate Video — soft circuits, conductive thread, LED garments
  • Adafruit wearables guides — Foundation Intermediate Tutorial — extensive, with sewing patterns
  • Circuit Playground Express projects — Foundation Tutorial — alligator-clip pads sew directly
  • Kitronik e-textiles resources — Foundation Tutorial — UK, classroom-tested

Parts: Circuit Playground Express or micro:bit, conductive thread, sewable LEDs, coin cell holders, LiPo (see safety).

docs.title: 🌱 Environment & sensing
docs.text:
The theme that connects best to science curricula — data logging drops straight into a physics or geography scheme of work.

  • Raspberry Pi Foundation — weather station projects — Intermediate Tutorial
  • Pimoroni Enviro guides — Intermediate Tutorial — air quality, temperature, light
  • Random Nerd Tutorials — sensors — Intermediate Tutorial — huge library, ESP32 and Pico
  • Adafruit STEMMA QT sensor guides — Intermediate Tutorial — keyed connectors, no miswiring
  • Sensor.Community — Intermediate Tutorial — build an air quality sensor and join a global open-data network. Real data, real contribution.

Progression: read a sensor → log to a file → graph it → publish to a dashboard → compare with public data → notice something nobody told you to notice.

That last step is where it stops being an exercise.

docs.title: 🎮 Games & retro computing
docs.text:
• Pico-8 style handhelds — Pimoroni PicoSystem guides — Intermediate Tutorial
  • RetroPie documentation — Intermediate Tutorial — emulation on a Pi. Discuss ROM legality explicitly; it's a genuinely useful conversation about copyright.
  • Raspberry Pi Foundation — game projects — Foundation Tutorial — Scratch through Python
  • Ben Eater — 6502 computer — Advanced Video — build the machine, then program it in assembly
  • Bitluni — Advanced Video — VGA and audio from microcontrollers that shouldn't manage it

docs.title: 🎵 Music & sound
docs.text:
Underused, and a strong hook for learners who don't see themselves as "technical".

  • Adafruit — MIDI and audio guides — Intermediate Tutorial
  • Sonic Pi — Foundation Tutorial — live-coded music, free, ships with Raspberry Pi OS, with excellent built-in tutorials. One of the fastest routes from zero to something a teenager wants to show a friend.
  • micro:bit music projects — Foundation Tutorial — v2 has a speaker onboard
  • Mozzi audio library — Advanced GitHub — synthesis on Arduino

Projects: MIDI controller · theremin from an ultrasonic sensor · step sequencer with LEDs · drum machine · guitar pedal (battery-powered only)

docs.title: 👁️ AI & computer vision
docs.text:
Where the advanced track gets genuinely exciting — and where the honest conversation about what these systems are and aren't belongs.

  • Picamera2 examples — Advanced GitHub
  • OpenCV tutorials — Advanced Tutorial — free and thorough
  • Edge Impulse — Advanced Tutorial — train and deploy ML to microcontrollers; free developer tier
  • Teachable Machine — Foundation Tutorial — train an image classifier in a browser in ten minutes, then export it. The best available demonstration of why training data matters, because learners immediately see their own bias in the results.
  • TensorFlow Lite Micro — Advanced GitHub

Teaching note: Teachable Machine at Foundation level, deliberately trained badly, is one of the most valuable half-hours you can spend with an 11-year-old. Show them a classifier that only recognises faces like theirs, and the concept of dataset bias lands permanently.

docs.title: 🏠 Home automation & IoT
docs.text:
• Random Nerd Tutorials — ESP32 IoT — Intermediate Tutorial — the deepest free library here
  • Home Assistant — Advanced Tutorial — open-source hub, runs on a Pi, extensive free docs
  • MQTT / Mosquitto — Advanced Reference — the messaging pattern most IoT projects need
  • Pi My Life Up — Intermediate Tutorial — Pi-hole, media servers, useful household things

⚠️ Mains switching is off-limits for under-18s. Use commercial smart plugs controlled over WiFi, never hand-built relay boards. See safety.

docs.title: 🚀 Space, flight & high altitude
docs.text:
The highest-ceiling theme, and the one that most reliably produces a university personal statement.

  • ESA CanSat — Advanced Curriculum — build a satellite in a drinks can, launch it, recover data. Runs nationally across Europe including the UK.
  • Raspberry Pi Foundation — Astro Pi — Intermediate Advanced Curriculum — write code that runs on the ISS. Free, and genuinely open to school teams. Mission Zero is achievable in a single lesson.
  • UKHAS wiki — Advanced Reference — UK high-altitude ballooning. Note the CAA permissions and licensing requirements before planning anything.
  • ArduPilot — Advanced GitHub — autonomous vehicle firmware

⚠️ UK drone rules (CAA) apply from very low weights and require registration and a flyer ID. Balloon launches need CAA permission. Build this into the project plan from day one rather than discovering it later.

docs.title: Cross-theme note
docs.text:
The best projects usually sit at an intersection. A plant monitor that tweets is environment plus IoT. A robot that recognises colours is robotics plus vision. A light-up jacket that reacts to music is wearables plus sound.

When a learner stalls, moving sideways into an adjacent theme usually restarts them faster than pushing harder on the current one.
